summary: Specifies using Digital Transmission Content Protection (DTCP) certificates as an authorization data type in the TLS authorization extension, following the guidelines in RFC 5878. It lets devices show DTCP credentials as part of a TLS handshake.

plainLanguage.summary: Many televisions, tablets and set-top boxes carry a certificate that the cable industry uses to protect premium video streams. This document lets such a device present that certificate during the secure connection setup, so a web service can see which device it is talking to.

questions: how does tls authorization data work
subtitle: How a device can present its DTCP certificate during a TLS handshake, using the TLS authorization extensions.

tldr.problem: Many consumer electronics devices hold DTCP certificates issued by the DTLA, but there was no standard way to present one to a web service during a TLS handshake.
tldr.mechanism: The document registers a new TLS authorization data type, dtcp_authorization(66). The server sends a 32-byte random nonce in a SupplementalData message, and the client answers with its DTCP certificate and a signature made with the private key of that certificate.
tldr.outcome: A server can learn which DTCP-certified device it is talking to, for example to verify supported features; what it then does with that is outside the scope of the document. It is an Informational Independent Submission and has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 7562 is an Informational Independent Submission, so it is not an Internet Standard. It has been updated by RFC 8996 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why DTCP Certificates in TLS
sections.content:
RFC 5878 introduces extensions that enable TLS to operate in environments where authorization information needs to be exchanged between the client and the server before any protected data is exchanged, which lets both sides decide what to exchange based on that information. This document, an Independent Submission, uses that machinery for Digital Transmission Content Protection (DTCP) certificates issued by the Digital Transmission Licensing Administrator (DTLA).

A substantial number of deployed consumer electronics devices, such as televisions, tablets, game consoles and set-top boxes, contain these certificates. They enable the secure transmission of premium audiovisual content between devices over various types of links, and they can also be used to verify device functionality, such as supported device features.

The goal is to let a DTCP-enabled device authenticate and authorize with its DTCP certificate when it accesses services over the Internet, for example web applications on televisions that enable value-added services. The DTCP certificate is not an X.509 certificate, but it can be cryptographically tied to the X.509 certificate used to establish the TLS session by an Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EC-DSA) signature. The actual semantics of the authorization decision by the client or server are beyond the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Many televisions, tablets and set-top boxes carry a certificate that the cable industry uses to protect premium video streams. This document lets such a device present that certificate during the secure connection setup, so a web service can see which device it is talking to.

sections.title: The Building Blocks
sections.content:
DTCP certificates come in three general variations. Format 0 is the Restricted Authentication device certificate format, typically issued to devices with limited computation resources. Format 1 is the Baseline Full Authentication format and is the most commonly issued one; it includes a unique DeviceID and a device EC-DSA public and private key pair generated by the DTLA. Format 2 is the Extended Full Authentication format, issued to devices that possess additional functions such as additional channel ciphers or specific device properties, and it also includes a unique DeviceID and a device EC-DSA key pair.

The mechanism specified in this document allows only Formats 1 and 2 to be exchanged in the SupplementalData message, since it requires the use of the EC-DSA private key associated with the certificate.

Two existing pieces of TLS are reused. RFC 4680 defines the SupplementalData handshake message. RFC 5878 defines the client_authz (7) and server_authz (8) extension types, which a hello message uses to say that the sender will send authorization data and receive it in SupplementalData messages, and it establishes a registry of authorization data formats that IANA maintains. This document adds one more format to that registry.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of DTCP certificate, but only the two that come with a private key can be used here, because the exchange needs that key to sign. TLS already has a handshake message, called SupplementalData, for carrying extra data, and the certificate travels in it.

sections.title: The DTCP Authorization Data
sections.content:
The new type in the TLS Authorization Data Formats registry is dtcp_authorization(66). When it is in use, the authorization data is a dtcp_authz_data structure with four parts.

  • The RandomNonce is 32 bytes generated by a high-quality, secure random number generator. The server generates it and the client always sends it back. It helps the server detect replay attacks.
  • The DTCPCert is the sender's DTCP certificate.
  • The ASN.1Cert is the sender's certificate used to establish the TLS session, sent in the Certificate or ClientCertificate message. If it is not sent, its length MUST be zero.
  • The signature covers the nonce, the DTCP certificate and the ASN.1 certificate if present. It is generated with the private key associated with the DTCP certificate, which provides proof of the possession of that key by the sender. A sender sending its own DTCP certificate MUST populate this field.

The length of the signature field is determined by the Signature Algorithm and Hash Algorithm, so it is not explicitly encoded in the structure; the RFC gives 40 bytes for a SHA1 and ECDSA algorithm combination as an example. The two certificates are variable-length vectors, so the actual length precedes the contents in the byte stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The message holds four things: a random number made up by the server, the DTCP certificate, the X.509 certificate used for the session, and a signature. The signature is made with the private key that belongs to the DTCP certificate, so it shows that the sender really owns the certificate.

sections.title: Client and Server Rules
sections.content:
A client that wants to exchange DTCP authorization data includes both the client_authz and server_authz extensions in its ClientHello, and puts the dtcp_authorization format in the extension data field. A server that agrees answers with both extensions in its ServerHello. If the client's hello message does not contain both the client_authz and server_authz extensions with the dtcp_authorization type, the server MUST NOT include support for dtcp_authorization data in its hello message.

The server speaks first. It MUST generate and populate the RandomNonce, because at that point it cannot know whether the client will send an X.509 certificate. A server MAY include its own DTCP certificate; if it does not, it sends only the RandomNonce. If it does include one, it MUST also include its server certificate, which ties the data to the TLS session being established and helps the client detect replay attacks.

The client receives the server's dtcp_authz_data before it sends its own, and it includes the same RandomNonce that it received. Clients MUST include their DTCP certificate, and MAY include their ASN.1 certificate to tie the data to the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends the random number first, because it cannot yet know whether the client has a certificate of its own. The client then answers with that same number, its DTCP certificate and the signature.

sections.title: Alerts and the IANA Registration
sections.content:
Errors reuse existing TLS alert messages. A client sends unsupported_extension, which is always fatal, when it receives a server hello message that includes support for dtcp_authorization in only one of client_authz or server_authz but not in both. Omitting the dtcp_authorization extension, or omitting client_authz and server_authz completely, is allowed and is not a reason to send the alert. Either side sends certificate_unknown when it has received an X.509 certificate in the dtcp_authorization data that does not match the certificate sent in the corresponding ClientCertificate or Certificate message.

IANA maintains a TLS Authorization Data Formats registry, defined by RFC 5878, with one range for IETF Review and another for Specification Required. The value for dtcp_authorization is to be assigned by Specification Required under RFC 5226. The extension is compatible with Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS), RFC 6347, and the registry assignment is marked Y for DTLS-OK.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the two sides use the warning messages TLS already has. The new data format is also entered in the official registry of TLS authorization formats, under the number 66.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The dtcp_authorization data carries the DTCP certificate that identifies the associated device, and including the X.509 certificate used to establish the TLS session allows an application to tie the two together cryptographically. A TLS client, however, is not required to use and may not possess an X.509 certificate. In that case the exchange is prone to a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack, and a TLS server MUST deny access to the application features that depend on the DTCP certificate, or use a double handshake.

The double handshake mechanism is itself vulnerable to the TLS MITM Renegotiation exploit described in RFC 5746, so clients and servers MUST use the secure_renegotiation extension when exchanging dtcp_authorization data. The renegotiation is also vulnerable to the Triple Handshake exploit, so servers MUST use the same ASN.1 certificate during renegotiation as the one used in the initial handshake.

Any extension that changes the TLS handshake sequence, such as the TLS Session Ticket of RFC 5077, may result in failure to exchange SupplementalData, which would break the double handshake. The security considerations of RFC 5878 and RFC 5246 apply to the extension, and the dtcp_authorization data may be carried along with other supplemental data or other authorization data that requires additional protection.
sections.plainLanguage: If the client has no X.509 certificate of its own, someone could sit in the middle of the exchange and pretend. In that case the server must either refuse the features that depend on the DTCP certificate or run a second handshake, and both sides must use the secure renegotiation extension that protects that second handshake.

items.title: Format 0
items.text: Restricted Authentication. Typically issued to devices with limited computation resources.

items.title: Format 1
items.text: Baseline Full Authentication. The most commonly issued format; it carries a unique DeviceID and a device EC-DSA key pair.

items.title: Format 2
items.text: Extended Full Authentication. Issued to devices with additional functions; it also carries a unique DeviceID and a device EC-DSA key pair.
